questions.prompt: After Chapter 13 studies dynamics, what does Chapter 14 add?
choices: Why systems resist change or decay for structural reasons
Why timing is the only thing that matters
Why people are usually the whole problem
questions.explanation: Chapter 14 turns from movement to the structural forces that keep old paths alive or let coherence decay.

questions.prompt: What does inertia mean in this chapter?
choices: Built-in resistance to change inside the structure
Simple laziness by a few people
Any delay that appears during planning
questions.explanation: Inertia is structural weight that makes the old path easier to continue and redirection more costly.

questions.prompt: Which mistake does the chapter criticize?
choices: Diagnosing structure before blaming people
Treating moral complaint as enough explanation for resistance
Looking for where coherence is leaking away
questions.explanation: The chapter warns that blame often hides the real obstacle when drag and resistance are built into the system.

questions.prompt: A school program stays busy but keeps getting softer because handoffs, standards, and focus are slipping. What is the Chapter 14 diagnosis?
choices: Healthy momentum
Entropy weakening coherence over time
Proof that no structure matters
questions.explanation: Entropy means drift, decay, and loss of coherence even without obvious sabotage.

choices: Because systems can lose sharpness over time unless coherence is renewed
Because entropy only matters after complete collapse
Because visible effort automatically prevents decay
questions.explanation: The chapter emphasizes that drift and leakage can soften a system long before collapse is obvious.

choices: By abandoning trajectories and returning to snapshots
By explaining why some trajectories harden or degrade
By treating movement as enough on its own
questions.explanation: Chapter 13 showed that paths matter; Chapter 14 explains why some paths become sticky or lose coherence.

questions.prompt: A household keeps falling into the old routine even after everyone agrees to change. What concept fits best?
choices: Structural inertia
Proof that no one really cares
Evidence that goals are unnecessary
questions.explanation: The old pattern survives because the structure still makes it easier than the new one.

questions.prompt: What is the best sign that drag is structural?
choices: The same bad path keeps reproducing because the system rewards it
A one-time disagreement appears in a meeting
People ask for clearer direction
questions.explanation: Structural drag shows up when the arrangement itself keeps recreating the unwanted behavior.

questions.prompt: Why are good intentions not enough in this chapter?
choices: Because structure can still resist change and drift can still weaken coherence
Because intentions never matter
Because the only answer is blame
questions.explanation: People may want the right outcome and still fail if inertia and entropy keep working underneath.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter point toward the synthesis chapter?
choices: Because once structure is diagnosed, strategy can combine direction, counterforce, and coherent action
Because final synthesis no longer needs diagnosis
Because the book stops caring about resistance and drift
questions.explanation: Chapter 14 sets up the final integration by showing that strategy has to diagnose and counter structural drag and decay.
